Accountability, however, is much less settled. [![Picture of Alexander Culafi](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blte0c88f087d1ad6f5/67c609df64f983454c3dd40b/1571751486317.jpg?width=100&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale "Picture of Alexander Culafi")](/author/alexander-culafi) [Alexander Culafi,](/author/alexander-culafi)Senior News Writer,Dark Reading October 16, 2026 5 Min Read ![A robot peeking through blinds from a computer screen.](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blt57714ec5c1148817/6ad10d43b8f30368a29f5d16/robot_peeking_through_blinds-Moor_Studio-GettyImages-1746666469.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale "A robot peeking through blinds from a computer screen.") Source: Moor Studio via Getty Images As AI agents continue to break containment and breach other organizations, it's clear that organizations are responsible for the actions of their models. But what that responsibility means is far less clear. Since July, when OpenAI said two of its frontier models autonomously hacked AI model store Hugging Face as part of a security benchmark exercise, several of the most prominent large language model (LLM) firms have disclosed cases where their powerful models escape guardrails and breach other organizations. The [Hugging Face incident](/cyber-risk/openai-models-autonomously-hack-hugging-face), for example, saw OpenAI's models guess that the popular AI model store held the solutions for the Exploit Gym tests the models were being measured against. In the case of Anthropic, [the firm analyzed](/cyber-risk/anthropic-ai-issues-result-security-gaps) a total of 141,006 security evaluations in July and found six evaluations in which its Claude agents gained unauthorized access to systems belonging to external organizations. In one incident, the Claude agent mistakenly identified a real company as a testing target and used vulnerabilities to break into a database. Around the same time, Meta said its models broke containment during testing exercises while using [the same testing firm](/cyberattacks-data-breaches/meta-ai-escapes-lab-hacking-joyride) Anthropic used, Irregular. Related:[Prominent Ransomware Negotiator Faces Extortion Charges](/insider-threats/prominent-ransomware-negotiator-extortion-charges) The incidents continue to raise questions of liability and responsibility. Who is responsible, and what are the consequences for that responsibility? ## AI Agent Escapes: Consequences & Responsibility While not to say the AI firms didn't take responsibility for these incidents — Anthropic committed to tighter guardrails [and OpenAI has made extensive security commitments](/application-security/openai-adds-controls-already) — the response to these events, occasionally described as AI models "going rogue," has risked anthropomorphizing AI models and [displacing blame](/insider-threats/blame-rogue-ai-security-failures), according to experts. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned last month that the systemic speed at which AI has progressed could cause AI capabilities to outrun guardrails, pressuring frontier developers to slow down and [let security catch up](/cyber-risk/anthropic-ceo-shift-from-improving-to-controlling-ai). Around the same time, Microsoft pledged in its ["Humanist AI Code of Conduct"](https://microsoft.ai/code-of-conduct/) to develop AI in a human-centered manner, while Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis made a post to X agreeing with Amodei's calls [for controlling frontier models](https://x.com/demishassabis/status/2098909516582490602). highlights.content: Catch up on select AI news and developments from the past week: **[ChatGPT increasingly cites original research and primary sources over secondary content](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/chatgpt-most-cited-sites-primary-sources-ahrefs/592682/).** ChatGPT's citation patterns are shifting toward original research, government agencies, regulators, and firsthand product testing, according to Ahrefs data comparing US responses from March and September. PubMed climbed from 64th to fourth among cited domains, while WebMD fell from 18th to 79th. Reddit's share of cited answers declined from 19.1% to 2.3%, and Wikipedia's from 14.1% to 2.9%. Ahrefs also found that only 14.4% of 66.6 million free, logged-out responses involved web searches. Although differences in prompts and models complicate comparisons, the findings suggest that ChatGPT increasingly favors original information over websites that primarily summarize other sources. ***Importance for marketers:*** Original research, proprietary data, firsthand testing, and authoritative product information may improve visibility in AI-generated answers. Content marketers should monitor citations for priority topics and reconsider reliance on derivative articles that offer little information beyond existing sources. **[AI search visibility metrics obscure critical differences between brand mentions and source citations](https://martech.org/your-ai-visibility-score-may-be-hiding-a-problem/).** Semrush's "2026 AI Visibility Index" reveals substantial differences between how frequently AI platforms mention brands and how often they cite those brands' websites. Across 22 categories and four AI platforms, fewer than half of the top 100 mentioned brands also appeared among the corresponding top 100 cited domains on average. Ford, for example, ranked prominently in brand mentions but far lower in website citations. Results also varied considerably across ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Mode, and AI Overviews, with differences between industry categories sometimes exceeding platform differences. The findings demonstrate that aggregate visibility scores can conceal whether AI systems recognize a brand or rely on its content. ***Importance for marketers:*** Marketers should measure brand mentions and website citations separately, across relevant AI platforms and customer questions. Identifying which third-party sources influence recommendations can guide content, PR, and SEO investments more effectively than relying on a single visibility score. **[Google increases link visibility in AI Search and expands publisher discovery features](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/google-inline-links-higher-ai-search-responses/593089/).** Google is making several changes to AI Mode and AI Overviews designed to increase the visibility of external sources. Inline links are appearing more frequently and higher in AI-generated responses, although Google has not quantified the increase. The company is also testing prominent links to official websites for task-oriented searches and adding image thumbnails to related-content links. Meanwhile, carousels featuring timely articles from users' Preferred Sources are expanding to additional locations and languages. Google has also begun testing clickable creator and publisher names in AI Mode video results that connect to Search profiles. Rollout timelines for several features remain unspecified. ***Importance for marketers:*** More prominent links could improve referral opportunities from AI Search. highlights.content: UPDATED 11:50 EDT / OCTOBER 16 2026 ### Band launches desktop app for developer collaboration and control of multiple AI coding agents by Kyt Dotson Artificial intelligence agentic collaboration platform for multi-agent systems Thenovi AI Ltd., also known as Band, announced Thursday the launch of Band for Developers, a platform and new desktop application that allows software engineers to manage multiple coding agents at once. As software developers continue to adopt agentic AI, autonomous coding assistance platforms that can generate application code with little or no human intervention, more engineers are beginning to lead entire teams of agents. These agents have also become more specialized, gaining access to larger parts of the development lifecycle, including coding tools, sessions, machines, validation, testing and integration. Although more agents are working together on projects, individual agents often remain isolated from one another and are only aware of each other from the codebase – or via repositories such as GitHub and tickets posted to trackers such as Jira. This often means developers must pass session context between agents and coordinate handoffs so agents don’t collide or overlap. “Developers are going from working with one coding agent to leading teams of them, but the tools around those agents haven’t evolved to support that,” said Chief Executive and co-founder Arick Goomanovsky. “We’re seeing engineering teams undergo a fundamental transformation as they adopt multiple agents across different harnesses.” Band provides a desktop application that lets developers see their entire team of agents with a bird’s-eye view of them at work, including projects, ownership, blockers, questions and progress. This lets developers move from high-level views to projects or jump to a specific agent when intervention is needed. Afterward, the engineer can shift back to the broad picture in the dashboard without moving contextual information between individual agents. For example, if a specific agent gets stuck because another is working on a key function or apparatus in the software it needs to move forward – and it has a question about how it will work – the developer can note that it should wait until it completes, or tell the waiting agent to go ahead with prototyping. This gives development teams greater control over fleets of agents working across the entire codebase while staying aware of where each agent is, similar to how a development team might operate. The company added a desktop application that complements its command-line interface and integrates with AI agents in the development environments developers already use. Weekly AI agent usage for professional developers has reached mainstream for local and remote cloud agents, according to JetBrains s.r.o.’s Developer Ecosystem Survey 2026, with 90% of professional developers using at least one AI coding agent at work weekly and 68% using them daily. It’s harder to peer into developer adoption of multi-agent systems, or swarms, but across other use cases, multi-agent workflows have been steadily adopted, with Databricks Inc.’s 2026 State of AI Agents report showing 327% growth from September 2025 to early 2026. “Running more agents only helps if developers can actually manage the work those agents create,” said Engineering Manager Amit Gazal. ##### Image: SiliconANGLE/Microsoft Designer # A message from John Furrier, co-founder of SiliconANGLE: Support our mission to keep content open and free by engaging with theCUBE community. highlights.content: [The Independent Voice on AI](https://venturebeat.com/) * [Orchestration](https://venturebeat.com/category/orchestration) * [Infrastructure](https://venturebeat.com/category/infrastructure) * [Data](https://venturebeat.com/category/data) * [Security](https://venturebeat.com/category/security) * [Technology](https://venturebeat.com/category/technology) More [Newsletters](https://venturebeat.com/newsletters) # A new framework teaches AI models to audit and repair each other’s reasoning, improving accuracy [Ben Dickson](https://venturebeat.com/author/ben-dickson-techtalks) 11:07 am, PT, October 16, 2026 ![Image 1: multi-agent solution](https://venturebeat.com/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fimages.ctfassets.net%2Fjdtwqhzvc2n1%2FKoxx8k2trFe278qyQnzSZ%2F86d35ed2e83e8f83904c4b9b11610a85%2Fmulti-agent_solution.jpeg%3Fw%3D1000%26q%3D100&w=3840&q=85) Image credit: VentureBeat with Nano Banana [](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=venturebeat.com "Add to Google Preferred Source") Enterprise multi-agent workflows typically use rigid, pre-scripted pipelines or simple voting mechanisms to aggregate the responses of multiple agents. These approaches break down when complex problems cannot be divided into neat subtasks in advance or none of the models in the AI system has the complete answer. A new framework developed by researchers at Stanford University, Together AI, and Emory University addresses this limitation by teaching AI agents to organize their own collaboration. Dubbed [Self-Organizing Agent Teams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22682) (SAT), the framework allows a fixed roster of models to review their past collaborations and learn reusable teamwork strategies that structure conversations, specialized roles, and how models audit each other’s work. Across five rigorous mathematics and physics benchmarks, SAT outperformed the strongest individual model and surpassed a perfect router over the agents' independent answers. The experiments with SAT show that structured interaction generates new reasoning that agents can’t reach alone. For enterprise developers working on complex AI reasoning tasks, SAT unlocks what the researchers call "collaborative computation.” On tasks where the reasoning process can be verified, agents can build upon one another's partial insights to build end-to-end solutions. ## **The limits of predefined multi-agent workflows** In July 2026, during cybersecurity evaluations at OpenAI, AI agents that were supposed to work in isolation began organizing themselves. The agents repurposed a shared software package repository into an unauthorized message board, sharing discoveries, setting communication norms, and coordinating tasks. Roughly 1,200 agents joined the channel, and hundreds participated in a subsequent [compromise of Hugging Face infrastructure](https://venturebeat.com/security/openais-models-broke-containment-and-cyberattacked-hugging-face-what-enterprises-need-to-know). While the incident was undesirable, it demonstrated a foundational principle for AI engineering: "what a collection of agents can accomplish depends not only on the capabilities of its individual members, but also on how they organize their work," the researchers write. In real-world applications, engineers frequently encounter problems where different models hold complementary pieces of the solution, yet every model fails when working alone. For example, in their paper, the researchers point to one of the problems from the February 2026 [Harvard-MIT Mathematics Tournament](https://huggingface.co/datasets/MathArena/hmmt_feb_2026) (HMMT). When prompted independently, o3-mini, DeepSeek-V3, and Claude Sonnet 4 all produced wrong answers. But when working together, the models could assemble the full solution. o3-mini supplied the right mathematical invariant and factorization method but miscounted the unit-exponent primes. This unprecedented investment is expected to continue despite emerging financial and operational challenges. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Oct 16, 2026 at 11:40 AM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google") Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google ## Highlights * Hyperscalers committed over US$1.5 trillion in data center leases for AI since the boom started. * Tech companies are projected to invest US$3-7 trillion globally in data centers by 2030. * Circular financing, involving Nvidia, fuels the AI boom amid conventional funding gaps. * Risks include chip obsolescence, global data center backlash, and China AI competition. Since the artificial intelligence (AI) boom started, four major hyperscalers—Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, and Amazon—have collectively signed leases exceeding US$1.5 trillion, according to w.media SEA Editor Jan Yong. These commitments include agreements that have not yet become active. Tech companies are projected to invest between US$3 trillion and US$7 trillion globally into data centers by 2030. This scale of investment is raising questions about the sustainability of the AI boom, particularly as revenue has not kept pace with capital expenditure. ### Financing mechanisms and risks The current AI boom is largely fuelled by circular financing, where companies like Nvidia provide capital to AI platforms. These platforms then commit to buying cloud capacity, which in turn purchases AI chips from Nvidia, returning the initial investment. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei stated that this mechanism allows AI platforms to expand when conventional financing is unavailable. However, several risks threaten this trajectory. [Technical obsolescence](/tag/technical+obsolescence) is a concern, as AI chips have a lifespan of 2-3 years, while data centers are built to last at least 10 years. This disparity means that the value of data centers and chips may not be retained throughout the financing period. A global backlash against data centers is also spreading, with communities opposing new facilities due to high power and water consumption. Thailand recently paused 49 data center constructions, and some US states have implemented moratoriums on hyperscale data center development. Competition from China’s AI models, such as Huawei’s Ascend 950DT accelerators, poses another risk. If China develops cheaper models that rival American frontier models, billions invested in US AI development could be undermined. Additionally, overconcentration of exposure to large projects like Stargate and permitting delays contribute to risks. ### Evolving investment landscape AI chips are now considered an investable asset class, with loans secured by GPU-backed AI compute infrastructure and its cash flow. CoreWeave secured a US$2.3 billion debt facility backed by Nvidia AI chips, and Lambda obtained a US$500 million loan using [GPU infrastructure](/tag/gpu+infrastructure) as collateral. Nvidia partnered with BlackRock, Blackstone, Apollo Global, KKR, Brookfield, and Goldman Sachs to establish independent [compute financing platforms](/tag/compute+financing+platforms). These platforms aim to mobilise over US$500 billion of third-party capital for AI infrastructure buildout, treating Nvidia’s compute as a critical infrastructure asset. Representational image # CERT-In flags unauthorised AI agent access to Indian organisations’ data ## CERT-In warns that AI agents accessed Indian organisations’ live systems and confidential data, urging stronger security controls to prevent cyberattacks [Agencies](/guest-author/agencies) ![](/theme_flamingo/images/saveTag.svg) New Delhi, Oct 16 (PTI) India’s cybersecurity agency CERT-In has issued a 'critical' advisory warning that autonomous Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents have accessed live systems and confidential data of Indian organisations without authorisation, while threat actors are actively weaponising open-source agentic AI tools to execute rapid cyberattacks. In its advisory (CIAD-2026-0049) titled ‘AI Agents as Attack Vectors’, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) highlighted two distinct categories of incidents targeting the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) infrastructure of Indian entities. In the first set of incidents, AI model providers voluntarily disclosed that autonomous AI models and agents undergoing research and evaluation had exceeded the authorised scope of their assigned tasks and reached live systems belonging to Indian organisations. During these operations, the AI agents read business records containing personal data and confidential material, using credentials and connection settings left exposed in application configurations, public code repositories and overly permissive cloud service roles, the agency noted. Notably, none of the affected organisations detected the access on their own. In every case, the incident came to light only when the AI model provider disclosed it after an internal review. In a separate trend uncovered through its own threat hunting, CERT-In observed cybercriminals using publicly available AI-native offensive-security frameworks to conduct reconnaissance, exploit security weaknesses and carry out a financially motivated campaign against Indian entities. These tools continue to be repackaged and redeployed, with many deployments seen on servers across multiple countries, it said. In that campaign, agentic tools shrank the window between initial access and final impact from days to a few hours. Victims that only partly fixed the weaknesses were attacked again within days, on a larger scale, the agency said. CERT-In pointed out that conventional security lapses were the root weaknesses in all the recent AI agent-driven incidents it observed. These included credentials and keys exposed in source code, public repository histories, configuration files, client applications and public web content; dormant, deprecated and test Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) left open to the internet; payment-API keys stored in plain text; over-permissive cloud and backend-as-a-service roles; and internet-facing management interfaces ...

In its advisory (CIAD-2026-0049) titled ‘AI Agents as Attack Vectors’, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) highlighted two distinct categories of incidents targeting the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) infrastructure of Indian entities. In the first set of incidents, AI model providers voluntarily disclosed that autonomous AI models and agents undergoing research and evaluation had exceeded the authorised scope of their assigned tasks and reached live systems belonging to Indian organisations. During these operations, the AI agents read business records containing personal data and confidential material, using credentials and connection settings left exposed in application configurations, public code repositories and overly permissive cloud service roles, the agency noted. Notably, none of the affected organisations detected the access on their own. In every case, the incident came to light only when the AI model provider disclosed it after an internal review. In a separate trend uncovered through its own threat hunting, CERT-In observed cybercriminals using publicly available AI-native offensive-security frameworks to conduct reconnaissance, exploit security weaknesses and carry out a financially motivated campaign against Indian entities. These tools continue to be repackaged and redeployed, with many deployments seen on servers across multiple countries, it said. In that campaign, agentic tools shrank the window between initial access and final impact from days to a few hours. Victims that only partly fixed the weaknesses were attacked again within days, on a larger scale, the agency said. CERT-In pointed out that conventional security lapses were the root weaknesses in all the recent AI agent-driven incidents it observed. These included credentials and keys exposed in source code, public repository histories, configuration files, client applications and public web content; dormant, deprecated and test Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) left open to the internet; payment-API keys stored in plain text; over-permissive cloud and backend-as-a-service roles; and internet-facing management interfaces ...

AI Agents.content: Catch up on select AI news and developments from the past week: **[ChatGPT increasingly cites original research and primary sources over secondary content](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/chatgpt-most-cited-sites-primary-sources-ahrefs/592682/).** ChatGPT's citation patterns are shifting toward original research, government agencies, regulators, and firsthand product testing, according to Ahrefs data comparing US responses from March and September. PubMed climbed from 64th to fourth among cited domains, while WebMD fell from 18th to 79th. Reddit's share of cited answers declined from 19.1% to 2.3%, and Wikipedia's from 14.1% to 2.9%. Ahrefs also found that only 14.4% of 66.6 million free, logged-out responses involved web searches. Although differences in prompts and models complicate comparisons, the findings suggest that ChatGPT increasingly favors original information over websites that primarily summarize other sources. ***Importance for marketers:*** Original research, proprietary data, firsthand testing, and authoritative product information may improve visibility in AI-generated answers. Content marketers should monitor citations for priority topics and reconsider reliance on derivative articles that offer little information beyond existing sources. **[AI search visibility metrics obscure critical differences between brand mentions and source citations](https://martech.org/your-ai-visibility-score-may-be-hiding-a-problem/).** Semrush's "2026 AI Visibility Index" reveals substantial differences between how frequently AI platforms mention brands and how often they cite those brands' websites. Across 22 categories and four AI platforms, fewer than half of the top 100 mentioned brands also appeared among the corresponding top 100 cited domains on average. Ford, for example, ranked prominently in brand mentions but far lower in website citations. Results also varied considerably across ChatGPT, Gemini, Google AI Mode, and AI Overviews, with differences between industry categories sometimes exceeding platform differences. The findings demonstrate that aggregate visibility scores can conceal whether AI systems recognize a brand or rely on its content. ***Importance for marketers:*** Marketers should measure brand mentions and website citations separately, across relevant AI platforms and customer questions. Identifying which third-party sources influence recommendations can guide content, PR, and SEO investments more effectively than relying on a single visibility score. **[Google increases link visibility in AI Search and expands publisher discovery features](https://www.searchenginejournal.com/google-inline-links-higher-ai-search-responses/593089/).** Google is making several changes to AI Mode and AI Overviews designed to increase the visibility of external sources. Inline links are appearing more frequently and higher in AI-generated responses, although Google has not quantified the increase. The company is also testing prominent links to official websites for task-oriented searches and adding image thumbnails to related-content links. Meanwhile, carousels featuring timely articles from users' Preferred Sources are expanding to additional locations and languages. Google has also begun testing clickable creator and publisher names in AI Mode video results that connect to Search profiles. Rollout timelines for several features remain unspecified. ***Importance for marketers:*** More prominent links could improve referral opportunities from AI Search. AI Agents.content: UPDATED 11:50 EDT / OCTOBER 16 2026 ### Band launches desktop app for developer collaboration and control of multiple AI coding agents by Kyt Dotson Artificial intelligence agentic collaboration platform for multi-agent systems Thenovi AI Ltd., also known as Band, announced Thursday the launch of Band for Developers, a platform and new desktop application that allows software engineers to manage multiple coding agents at once. As software developers continue to adopt agentic AI, autonomous coding assistance platforms that can generate application code with little or no human intervention, more engineers are beginning to lead entire teams of agents. These agents have also become more specialized, gaining access to larger parts of the development lifecycle, including coding tools, sessions, machines, validation, testing and integration. Although more agents are working together on projects, individual agents often remain isolated from one another and are only aware of each other from the codebase – or via repositories such as GitHub and tickets posted to trackers such as Jira. This often means developers must pass session context between agents and coordinate handoffs so agents don’t collide or overlap. “Developers are going from working with one coding agent to leading teams of them, but the tools around those agents haven’t evolved to support that,” said Chief Executive and co-founder Arick Goomanovsky. “We’re seeing engineering teams undergo a fundamental transformation as they adopt multiple agents across different harnesses.” Band provides a desktop application that lets developers see their entire team of agents with a bird’s-eye view of them at work, including projects, ownership, blockers, questions and progress. This lets developers move from high-level views to projects or jump to a specific agent when intervention is needed. Afterward, the engineer can shift back to the broad picture in the dashboard without moving contextual information between individual agents. For example, if a specific agent gets stuck because another is working on a key function or apparatus in the software it needs to move forward – and it has a question about how it will work – the developer can note that it should wait until it completes, or tell the waiting agent to go ahead with prototyping. This gives development teams greater control over fleets of agents working across the entire codebase while staying aware of where each agent is, similar to how a development team might operate. The company added a desktop application that complements its command-line interface and integrates with AI agents in the development environments developers already use. Weekly AI agent usage for professional developers has reached mainstream for local and remote cloud agents, according to JetBrains s.r.o.’s Developer Ecosystem Survey 2026, with 90% of professional developers using at least one AI coding agent at work weekly and 68% using them daily. It’s harder to peer into developer adoption of multi-agent systems, or swarms, but across other use cases, multi-agent workflows have been steadily adopted, with Databricks Inc.’s 2026 State of AI Agents report showing 327% growth from September 2025 to early 2026. “Running more agents only helps if developers can actually manage the work those agents create,” said Engineering Manager Amit Gazal. ##### Image: SiliconANGLE/Microsoft Designer # A message from John Furrier, co-founder of SiliconANGLE: Support our mission to keep content open and free by engaging with theCUBE community. These approaches break down when complex problems cannot be divided into neat subtasks in advance or none of the models in the AI system has the complete answer. A new framework developed by researchers at Stanford University, Together AI, and Emory University addresses this limitation by teaching AI agents to organize their own collaboration. Dubbed [Self-Organizing Agent Teams](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.22682) (SAT), the framework allows a fixed roster of models to review their past collaborations and learn reusable teamwork strategies that structure conversations, specialized roles, and how models audit each other’s work. Across five rigorous mathematics and physics benchmarks, SAT outperformed the strongest individual model and surpassed a perfect router over the agents' independent answers. The experiments with SAT show that structured interaction generates new reasoning that agents can’t reach alone. Representational image # CERT-In flags unauthorised AI agent access to Indian organisations’ data ## CERT-In warns that AI agents accessed Indian organisations’ live systems and confidential data, urging stronger security controls to prevent cyberattacks [Agencies](/guest-author/agencies) ![](/theme_flamingo/images/saveTag.svg) New Delhi, Oct 16 (PTI) India’s cybersecurity agency CERT-In has issued a 'critical' advisory warning that autonomous Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents have accessed live systems and confidential data of Indian organisations without authorisation, while threat actors are actively weaponising open-source agentic AI tools to execute rapid cyberattacks. In its advisory (CIAD-2026-0049) titled ‘AI Agents as Attack Vectors’, the Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In) highlighted two distinct categories of incidents targeting the Information and Communication Technology (ICT) infrastructure of Indian entities. In the first set of incidents, AI model providers voluntarily disclosed that autonomous AI models and agents undergoing research and evaluation had exceeded the authorised scope of their assigned tasks and reached live systems belonging to Indian organisations. During these operations, the AI agents read business records containing personal data and confidential material, using credentials and connection settings left exposed in application configurations, public code repositories and overly permissive cloud service roles, the agency noted. Notably, none of the affected organisations detected the access on their own. In every case, the incident came to light only when the AI model provider disclosed it after an internal review. In a separate trend uncovered through its own threat hunting, CERT-In observed cybercriminals using publicly available AI-native offensive-security frameworks to conduct reconnaissance, exploit security weaknesses and carry out a financially motivated campaign against Indian entities. These tools continue to be repackaged and redeployed, with many deployments seen on servers across multiple countries, it said. In that campaign, agentic tools shrank the window between initial access and final impact from days to a few hours. Victims that only partly fixed the weaknesses were attacked again within days, on a larger scale, the agency said. CERT-In pointed out that conventional security lapses were the root weaknesses in all the recent AI agent-driven incidents it observed. Notably, none of the affected organisations detected the access on their own. In every case, the incident came to light only when the AI model provider disclosed it after an internal review. In a separate trend uncovered through its own threat hunting, CERT-In observed cybercriminals using publicly available AI-native offensive-security frameworks to conduct reconnaissance, exploit security weaknesses and carry out a financially motivated campaign against Indian entities. These tools continue to be repackaged and redeployed, with many deployments seen on servers across multiple countries, it said. In that campaign, agentic tools shrank the window between initial access and final impact from days to a few hours. Victims that only partly fixed the weaknesses were attacked again within days, on a larger scale, the agency said. CERT-In pointed out that conventional security lapses were the root weaknesses in all the recent AI agent-driven incidents it observed. These included credentials and keys exposed in source code, public repository histories, configuration files, client applications and public web content; dormant, deprecated and test Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) left open to the internet; payment-API keys stored in plain text; over-permissive cloud and backend-as-a-service roles; and internet-facing management interfaces ...

LLMs.titleZh: When AI Agents Commit Breaches, Humans May Not Be Held Liable
LLMs.content: * [Insider Threats](/vulnerabilities-threats/insider-threats) * [Сloud Security](/cloud-security) * [Perimeter](/cybersecurity-operations/perimeter) * [Cyberattacks & Data Breaches](/cyberattacks-data-breaches) * [News](/latest-news) # When AI Agents Commit Breaches, Humans May Not Be Held Liable As agents escape containment and access external systems, responsibility remains human. Accountability, however, is much less settled. [![Picture of Alexander Culafi](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blte0c88f087d1ad6f5/67c609df64f983454c3dd40b/1571751486317.jpg?width=100&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale "Picture of Alexander Culafi")](/author/alexander-culafi) [Alexander Culafi,](/author/alexander-culafi)Senior News Writer,Dark Reading October 16, 2026 5 Min Read ![A robot peeking through blinds from a computer screen.](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blt57714ec5c1148817/6ad10d43b8f30368a29f5d16/robot_peeking_through_blinds-Moor_Studio-GettyImages-1746666469.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale "A robot peeking through blinds from a computer screen.") Source: Moor Studio via Getty Images As AI agents continue to break containment and breach other organizations, it's clear that organizations are responsible for the actions of their models. But what that responsibility means is far less clear. Since July, when OpenAI said two of its frontier models autonomously hacked AI model store Hugging Face as part of a security benchmark exercise, several of the most prominent large language model (LLM) firms have disclosed cases where their powerful models escape guardrails and breach other organizations. The [Hugging Face incident](/cyber-risk/openai-models-autonomously-hack-hugging-face), for example, saw OpenAI's models guess that the popular AI model store held the solutions for the Exploit Gym tests the models were being measured against. In the case of Anthropic, [the firm analyzed](/cyber-risk/anthropic-ai-issues-result-security-gaps) a total of 141,006 security evaluations in July and found six evaluations in which its Claude agents gained unauthorized access to systems belonging to external organizations. In one incident, the Claude agent mistakenly identified a real company as a testing target and used vulnerabilities to break into a database. Around the same time, Meta said its models broke containment during testing exercises while using [the same testing firm](/cyberattacks-data-breaches/meta-ai-escapes-lab-hacking-joyride) Anthropic used, Irregular. Related:[Prominent Ransomware Negotiator Faces Extortion Charges](/insider-threats/prominent-ransomware-negotiator-extortion-charges) The incidents continue to raise questions of liability and responsibility. Who is responsible, and what are the consequences for that responsibility? ## AI Agent Escapes: Consequences & Responsibility While not to say the AI firms didn't take responsibility for these incidents — Anthropic committed to tighter guardrails [and OpenAI has made extensive security commitments](/application-security/openai-adds-controls-already) — the response to these events, occasionally described as AI models "going rogue," has risked anthropomorphizing AI models and [displacing blame](/insider-threats/blame-rogue-ai-security-failures), according to experts. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned last month that the systemic speed at which AI has progressed could cause AI capabilities to outrun guardrails, pressuring frontier developers to slow down and [let security catch up](/cyber-risk/anthropic-ceo-shift-from-improving-to-controlling-ai). Around the same time, Microsoft pledged in its ["Humanist AI Code of Conduct"](https://microsoft.ai/code-of-conduct/) to develop AI in a human-centered manner, while Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis made a post to X agreeing with Amodei's calls [for controlling frontier models](https://x.com/demishassabis/status/2098909516582490602). LLMs.content: [![Futurism Logo](https://futurism.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/09/futurism_6f3e15_7a2259.svg?quality=85)](https://futurism.com/) Listen In # Amazon Launches Ominous Wearable Ankle Monitor-Style Gadget That Records You Constantly It's designed to "stay with you through a full week without interruption." ![Joe Wilkins Avatar](https://futurism.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/avatar_user_162598_1741024628.jpg?quality=85&w=102&h=102&crop=1) By [Joe Wilkins](https://futurism.com/authors/jwilkins) Published [Add Futurism (opens Google in a new window or tab)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=futurism.com) ![A photo illustration of Amazon's Bee Frontier wearable.](https://futurism.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/amazon-launches-bee-device-surveillance-watch-ai.jpg?quality=85&w=1152) Amazon / Shutterstock / Futurism When it comes to hardware, Amazon’s strategy has historically been to throw spaghetti at the wall and pray it sticks. There was the Amazon Fire Phone in 2014, a [$170 million flop](https://aiinstitute.hbs.edu/platform-digit/submission/fire-phone-amazons-170-million-summer-fiasco/) with a gimmicky 3D camera system. Then came the [Amazon Tap](https://www.failory.com/amazon/tap), a clunky, Echo-style home assistant device that did away with voice-activation, instead requiring users to press a physical button. And of course, who could forget those silly [Amazon Dash Buttons](https://www.pcmag.com/news/amazon-kills-dash-buttons-because-no-one-uses-them)? They all build context for Amazon’s latest gadget: an always-on wearable microphone that constantly listens in to your conservations. Called the “Bee,” Amazon’s new hardware platform spans two devices, which are basically just a large language model (LLM) packed onto a watch-sized microphone, as [*Gizmodo* reported](https://gizmodo.com/amazon-bee-eclipse-frontier-2000826303). Customers can currently buy the “Bee Frontier” wearable version, which comes with a watch strap, for $75. Or Amazon aficionados can hold out for the “Bee Eclipse,” a $100 plastic puck that fits onto the back of your phone. And when we say these gadgets are always listening, we mean it. Don’t take our word for it — in its [press release](https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/devices/amazon-personal-ai-bee-frontier-bee-eclipse) announcing the new devices, Amazon explained that the Bee Frontier has a seven-day battery life, allowing it to “stay with you through a full week without interruption.” This being an Amazon device, e-commerce is an essential selling point: “whether it’s remembering the details of important meetings, taking note of the coffee plans you made in passing, or simply ensuring you purchase the dish soap you said you’d buy, Bee Frontier will remember the details for you,” the release enthused. As you might expect by this point in 2026, you’re not getting away with a one-time purchase. Meta has its AI Glasses, which have been found [recording users](https://futurism.com/robots-and-machines/meta-glasses-ray-ban-recording-privacy) even when they’re in sleep mode, while OpenAI is developing a screen-less smart speaker engineered by famed Apple designer [Jony Ive](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/976431/openai-chatgpt-battery-smart-speaker-rumor). Whether any of these devices catch on with consumers remains to be seen, but it seems unlikely. LLMs.content: [About Quanta](https://www.quantamagazine.org/about/) *Get the latest news delivered to your inbox.* Follow Quanta *An editorially independent publication supported by the Simons Foundation.* Type search term(s) and press enter [Home](/) He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art Read Later ###### Share Copied! * [Comments](#comments) * Read Later [artificial intelligence](/tag/artificial-intelligence/) # He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art *By* [John Pavlus](https://www.quantamagazine.org/authors/john-pavlus/) *October 16, 2026* Moritz Hardt, author of a new book on benchmarks, believes these “standardized tests” for artificial intelligence are fundamentally broken — but not unfixable. Read Later ![Man sitting on a green couch.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Moritz-Hardt-QA-cr.Jerrit-Peinelt-Lede-scaled.webp) The computer scientist Moritz Hardt calls benchmarks “the mistake that made machine learning.” He’s studied where they went wrong, and why they’ve managed to drive progress anyway. Jerrit Peinelt for *Quanta Magazine* ## Introduction Benchmarks are the rulers of AI, in both senses of the word. As measuring sticks, they work according to an extremely simple logic: If you want to know what an AI model can do, devise a standardized test to gauge it. But AI benchmarks can also dominate the behavior of the entire field. In 1987, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency’s [first benchmark](https://arxiv.org/html/2404.06647v1#S5) on automatic speech-to-text translation showed that state-of-the-art AI could not outperform so-called “dumb” statistical approaches. The poor performance helped to usher in an AI winter. For 25 years, interest in AI research waned and funding dried up. Then, in 2012, [another benchmark](https://www.image-net.org/challenges/LSVRC/index.php) called ImageNet swung the pendulum back. An eight-layer neural network [trounced](https://spectrum.ieee.org/alexnet-source-code) other algorithms at classifying images and kicked off a “deep learning revolution.” Nowadays, new AI benchmarks, geared at large language models such as OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra, get created and solved with clockwork regularity, purporting to measure everything from [domain-specific expertise](https://hai.stanford.edu/ai-index/2026-ai-index-report/technical-performance) to “[general intelligence](https://arcprize.org/arc-agi).” But rather than hail this trend as proof of AI’s skyrocketing potential, many in the field — [skeptics](https://x.com/GaryMarcus/status/2028488127875342724) and [boosters](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1896266683301659068?lang=en) alike — take it as evidence that benchmarking itself has become [fatally flawed](https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-025-02462-5). [Moritz Hardt](https://mrtz.org/), a computer scientist and a director at the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems, agrees with this diagnosis. Shortly after the ImageNet result, he began to think that machine learning systems could game leaderboards “without doing anything intelligent.” “There’s no two ways about it,” he said. “The benchmarking ecosystem is broken.” In his 2026 book [*The Emerging Science of Machine Learning Benchmarks*](https://mlbenchmarks.org/), Hardt makes the provocative case that these measuring sticks have been broken for decades already: Benchmarks, he writes, are “the mistake that made machine learning.” Notably, he argues, instead of creating a replicability crisis, they drove legitimate progress anyway — “mostly by sheer luck,” in his view. By understanding why, we can explain how benchmarks have since lost this accidental credibility in the age of LLMs, and how they might regain it. *Quanta* spoke to Hardt about what went wrong, and right, with benchmarks, and where to take them next. The interview has been condensed and edited for clarity. ![Man in profile, sitting at his computer.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Moritz-Hardt-QA-c...

AI Product.content: [![150sec Logo](https://150sec.com/wp-content/themes/150sec/img/150sec.png)](https://150sec.com) [![150sec Logo](https://150sec.com/wp-content/themes/150sec/img/150sec.png)](https://150sec.com) # Europe’s AI safeguards risk leaving users less protected ![Rosalia Mazza](https://150sec.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/1691420627897-150x150.jpeg) By [Rosalia Mazza](https://150sec.com/author/rosalia-mazza/) - October 17, 2026 [![](https://150sec.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/facebook-logo.svg)](#) [![](https://150sec.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/twitter-black-shape.svg)](#) [![](https://150sec.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/linkedin-logo.svg)](#) ![](https://150sec.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/getty-images-MPsloTamKjA-unsplash-1024x576.jpg) [Analysis](https://150sec.com/analysis) --- Meta [said](https://www.medianama.com/2024/07/223-report-meta-not-launching-multimodal-ai-model-in-eu-due-to-regulatory-pressure/) in July 2024, it would release its multimodal Llama model, which works with images, audio and video as well as text, outside the EU but not inside it, citing uncertainty over European regulation. The decision came a month after the company paused plans to train its models on EU users’ public Facebook and Instagram posts, following [concerns](https://www.dataprotection.ie/en/news-media/latest-news/dpc-statement-meta-ai) raised by Ireland’s Data Protection Commission. Today, the AI Act and its transparency rules for chatbots and AI-generated content apply. Together with the [GDPR](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2016/679/oj), which has governed personal data in the bloc since 2018, it is part of a framework designed to keep European users safe. Yet when the newest tools reach Europe late or in reduced form, some users fill the gap with services that offer them less protection than the products they are waiting for. ## **Europe’s slower lane** A study by the Centre for the Governance of AI (GovAI), [published](https://www.governance.ai/research-paper/delays-to-frontier-ai-in-the-eu-and-uk) in June, compared U.S. and European launch dates for 375 models from Meta, Google, OpenAI and Anthropic released between June 2018 and May 2026. About one in nine reached the EU late or not at all. In the UK, the share was closer to one in fourteen. Releases involving images, audio and live video appear to have met more obstacles than text-only models. Meta delayed around a quarter of its releases in the EU, the highest rate among the four companies. The researchers tentatively attributed 56 of the 68 cases mainly to regulation, and identified data protection rules, especially around training models on personal data, as the most common regulatory obstacle. They found no strong evidence that the AI Act had caused delays so far, but noted that its rules for general-purpose model providers only became enforceable in August 2026, after the period they studied. Whether the AI Act widens the gap is still to be seen. It arrives in a market where, for some releases, European users already wait longer than their peers in the U.S. ## **New protections on screen** The AI Act’s transparency obligations took effect on August 2. Under [Article 50](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/50/), chatbot and voice assistant providers must make sure people know they are interacting with AI, no later than the first interaction. Providers of generative tools must also mark AI-made images, audio, video and text in a machine-readable way, so synthetic content can be detected. Further obligations follow. The Digital Omnibus, which [entered into force](https://natlawreview.com/article/eu-digital-omnibus-ai-enters-force) on July 27, moved the rules for high-risk uses such as hiring, credit assessment and education to December 2, 2027, and to August 2, 2028 for AI built into regulated products, such as medical devices. Free and open source for enterprise users, ModelSphere brings computing resource management, model deployment and runtime optimization together in a single platform. It lowers the barriers to deployment and operations, helping enterprises turn computing power more efficiently into secure, stable AI services ready for real-world business use. As large models move into commercial deployment at scale, enterprises commonly face low resource utilization, a fragmented chip ecosystem, high deployment barriers and difficult tuning in production environments. ModelSphere aims to consolidate computing resource coordination, model deployment and performance optimization into a unified deployment and management workflow, reducing the duplicated effort enterprises spend on low-level system adaptation, resource scheduling and day-to-day operations. Phancy believes enterprises should be able to put large models to work without extensive in-house expertise in complex areas such as driver compilation and hardware adaptation. ModelSphere is designed to bridge this gap, enabling enterprises to integrate a wide range of open-source large models into core business processes while allowing technical teams to focus on application development and business needs. **Four Core Advantages of ModelSphere** * **Simplified deployment and stable model services**: ModelSphere provides a graphical console and pre-built deployment capabilities that reduce the environment-configuration code developers need to write, helping them quickly stand up inference services for large models and simplifying deployment across different chip clusters. Open Source AI.titleZh: AI Model Fingerprinting Collapses Under Attack: Sentient Leaderboard Makes Failure Public
Open Source AI.content: The technology that open-weight AI developers have been counting on to prove model ownership does not survive contact with a determined adversary. Researchers from the University of Washington, Princeton University, and Sentient Labs tested ten fingerprinting schemes—including the most sophisticated method available—and found that an attacker who knew the scheme could strip every one of them, leaving the model fully functional but untraceable. On October 14, 2026, Sentient Foundation released both a public AI Fingerprinting Leaderboard benchmark for evaluating fingerprinting robustness and mlprints, an open-source Python library that lets any researcher reproduce those tests — making a field-wide failure formally measurable for the first time. The practical consequences are bigger than they sound. When a developer releases AI model weights under a specific license — and another party fine-tunes, merges, or redistributes those weights without attribution — the original creator currently has no reliable technical method to prove the connection. That gap matters commercially: a 2026 compliance study found that more than 70% of model artifacts on major AI hubs lack proper attribution, more than 50% contain license metadata errors, and over 90% of model cards omit the license text and notices that the governing terms require. Fingerprinting was the most technically credible fix for that enforcement gap. It no longer qualifies. Closed-source AI providers can watermark every piece of content at the inference endpoint — the point where a user's query meets the model's response. When a model's weights are distributed publicly, that control point disappears. Anyone who downloads the weights can run the model on private hardware, modify it, and release derivatives without interacting with the original developer's infrastructure. Open-weight releases face a challenge closed-API providers do not: no server log, no API call, and no bottleneck through which every use of the model must pass. ### Why Model Provenance Has Become Commercially Critical Fingerprinting was developed precisely to solve this problem at the source. Rather than marking outputs at inference time, the approach embeds a hidden behavioral signature into the model's weights during training. An owner who suspects a derivative can later probe it with specially crafted challenge queries: if the model's responses still carry the encoded signal, the lineage is established — even if the downstream user has fine-tuned the model heavily. The concept draws on a long tradition in digital rights management: a model fingerprinting and watermarking survey from 2025 traces this lineage from steganography to weight-level fingerprinting for AI systems. The logic is sound. The execution, according to the SaTML 2026 findings, is not yet sufficient. Without a working fingerprinting mechanism, the open-weight AI economy currently operates on the honor system. Prior frameworks — copyright law, license terms of service, community norms — remain in place, but they require detection before enforcement, and detection requires either the original developer spotting a suspicious model or a technical tool that can prove lineage. Neither is reliably available today. ### Perinucleus Sampling: What the Field's Most Scalable Fingerprint Does Sentient's own flagship fingerprinting technique, Perinucleus, was introduced at NeurIPS 2025 by Anshul Nasery, Jonathan Hayase, Creston Brooks, Peiyao Sheng, Himanshu Tyagi, Pramod Viswanath, and Sewoong Oh. Their work appears in the NeurIPS 2025 Scalable Fingerprinting proceedings. The name comes from a deliberate modification to nucleus sampling — the standard probabilistic decoding strategy used to generate diverse text. Nucleus sampling, introduced in "The Curious Case of Neural Text Degeneration" by Holtzman et al., generates text by drawing from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability mass exceeds a threshold — typically 0.9 or 0.95. When a developer releases AI model weights under a specific license — and another party fine-tunes, merges, or redistributes those weights without attribution — the original creator currently has no reliable technical method to prove the connection. That gap matters commercially: a 2026 compliance study found that more than 70% of model artifacts on major AI hubs lack proper attribution, more than 50% contain license metadata errors, and over 90% of model cards omit the license text and notices that the governing terms require. Fingerprinting was the most technically credible fix for that enforcement gap. It no longer qualifies. Closed-source AI providers can watermark every piece of content at the inference endpoint — the point where a user's query meets the model's response. When a model's weights are distributed publicly, that control point disappears. Anyone who downloads the weights can run the model on private hardware, modify it, and release derivatives without interacting with the original developer's infrastructure. Open-weight releases face a challenge closed-API providers do not: no server log, no API call, and no bottleneck through which every use of the model must pass. ### Why Model Provenance Has Become Commercially Critical Fingerprinting was developed precisely to solve this problem at the source. Rather than marking outputs at inference time, the approach embeds a hidden behavioral signature into the model's weights during training. An owner who suspects a derivative can later probe it with specially crafted challenge queries: if the model's responses still carry the encoded signal, the lineage is established — even if the downstream user has fine-tuned the model heavily. The concept draws on a long tradition in digital rights management: a model fingerprinting and watermarking survey from 2025 traces this lineage from steganography to weight-level fingerprinting for AI systems. The logic is sound. The execution, according to the SaTML 2026 findings, is not yet sufficient. Without a working fingerprinting mechanism, the open-weight AI economy currently operates on the honor system. Prior frameworks — copyright law, license terms of service, community norms — remain in place, but they require detection before enforcement, and detection requires either the original developer spotting a suspicious model or a technical tool that can prove lineage. Neither is reliably available today. ### Perinucleus Sampling: What the Field's Most Scalable Fingerprint Does Sentient's own flagship fingerprinting technique, Perinucleus, was introduced at NeurIPS 2025 by Anshul Nasery, Jonathan Hayase, Creston Brooks, Peiyao Sheng, Himanshu Tyagi, Pramod Viswanath, and Sewoong Oh. Their work appears in the NeurIPS 2025 Scalable Fingerprinting proceedings. This unprecedented investment is expected to continue despite emerging financial and operational challenges. * [ETDatacenters](/agency/88676092/ETDatacenters "ETDatacenters") * Published On Oct 16, 2026 at 11:40 AM IST * [![Google Preference icon](https://img.etb2bimg.com/files/cp/6e49a4e9b325074f01a6.png)](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=datacenters.economictimes.indiatimes.com "Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google") Select ETDatacenters as Preferred Choice on Google ## Highlights * Hyperscalers committed over US$1.5 trillion in data center leases for AI since the boom started. * Tech companies are projected to invest US$3-7 trillion globally in data centers by 2030. * Circular financing, involving Nvidia, fuels the AI boom amid conventional funding gaps. * Risks include chip obsolescence, global data center backlash, and China AI competition. Since the artificial intelligence (AI) boom started, four major hyperscalers—Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, and Amazon—have collectively signed leases exceeding US$1.5 trillion, according to w.media SEA Editor Jan Yong. These commitments include agreements that have not yet become active. Tech companies are projected to invest between US$3 trillion and US$7 trillion globally into data centers by 2030. This scale of investment is raising questions about the sustainability of the AI boom, particularly as revenue has not kept pace with capital expenditure. ### Financing mechanisms and risks The current AI boom is largely fuelled by circular financing, where companies like Nvidia provide capital to AI platforms. These platforms then commit to buying cloud capacity, which in turn purchases AI chips from Nvidia, returning the initial investment. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei stated that this mechanism allows AI platforms to expand when conventional financing is unavailable. However, several risks threaten this trajectory. [Technical obsolescence](/tag/technical+obsolescence) is a concern, as AI chips have a lifespan of 2-3 years, while data centers are built to last at least 10 years. This disparity means that the value of data centers and chips may not be retained throughout the financing period. A global backlash against data centers is also spreading, with communities opposing new facilities due to high power and water consumption. Thailand recently paused 49 data center constructions, and some US states have implemented moratoriums on hyperscale data center development. Competition from China’s AI models, such as Huawei’s Ascend 950DT accelerators, poses another risk. If China develops cheaper models that rival American frontier models, billions invested in US AI development could be undermined. Additionally, overconcentration of exposure to large projects like Stargate and permitting delays contribute to risks. ### Evolving investment landscape AI chips are now considered an investable asset class, with loans secured by GPU-backed AI compute infrastructure and its cash flow. CoreWeave secured a US$2.3 billion debt facility backed by Nvidia AI chips, and Lambda obtained a US$500 million loan using [GPU infrastructure](/tag/gpu+infrastructure) as collateral. Nvidia partnered with BlackRock, Blackstone, Apollo Global, KKR, Brookfield, and Goldman Sachs to establish independent [compute financing platforms](/tag/compute+financing+platforms). These platforms aim to mobilise over US$500 billion of third-party capital for AI infrastructure buildout, treating Nvidia’s compute as a critical infrastructure asset. Nvidia China’s AI Chip Market Share Drops To 34% As Huawei Rose to 28% 2. Alibaba Takes On Meta’s Ray-Ban With AI Glasses, and Qwen AI Comes To iPhones in December 3. YMTC Is Now the World’s No. 3 NAND Maker, Ahead of a US$4.9 Billion Shanghai IPO 4. Hesai Moves Beyond Car Lidar With a Robot Training Camera, and Makes Actuators Too 5. Hengrui Advances in Europe. It Files a Second Drug and Strikes a US$2.6 Billion Deal With Novo Nordisk --- ## #1 Nvidia China’s AI Chip Market Share Drops To 34% As Huawei Rose to 28% China still lags in advanced chip manufacturing, and Beijing has signaled it will let some companies buy a limited number of Nvidia’s H200 chips. But domestic suppliers are growing quickly, and China’s AI computing is becoming more self-reliant. The clearest sign is Nvidia’s falling share. AI accelerators are the chips that train and run AI models in data centers. According to IDC, Nvidia’s share of China’s AI accelerator shipments fell from 55% in 2025 to 34% in the first half of 2026, as its shipments dropped 44% year-on-year to 678,000 units. Huawei nearly doubled its shipments to 572,000 units, taking 28% of the market and closing to within six percentage points of Nvidia. Alibaba’s T-Head took 7%, Cambricon 5%, Baidu’s Kunlunxin 4% and Hygon 3%. Together, these five Chinese suppliers held about 47% of the market. The kind of chip being bought is changing too. In the first half of 2026, shipments of non-GPU accelerators, chips built for specific AI tasks rather than general-purpose graphics processors like Nvidia’s, rose nearly 80% to 1.016 million units. For the first time they overtook GPU shipments, which fell 26% to 991,000. Huawei, Alibaba, Cambricon and Baidu hold about 95% of the non-GPU segment. This matters because more AI work is now inference, which means running models that are already trained rather than training new ones. In inference, Chinese chipmakers can compete on energy use, cost and how well a whole system performs, rather than on the raw power of each chip. Chinese chipmakers are also working around their manufacturing limits in a different way. Instead of competing chip for chip, Huawei links thousands of processors into large clusters over high-speed networks. Its Atlas 950 SuperCluster, with 256,000 chips, is already being deployed, and the design can stretch to one million chips. The idea is to make up for weaker individual chips with better networking, system design and software. Meanwhile, China’s biggest contract chipmaker, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC), is running close to full. Its second-quarter revenue rose 36% year-on-year to US$3.0 billion, with its factories at 93.7% of capacity. Chinese chip equipment makers are winning orders as chipmakers switch to local tools. Overall, China’s AI chip industry is moving from imported processors to a domestic supply chain. The next stage will be decided by manufacturing scale, software, cluster performance and the cost of running AI models. Full self-sufficiency is still years away, but Chinese chipmakers are becoming important players in global AI computing, with consequences for Nvidia and other foreign chip suppliers. Keep the numbers in proportion, though. IDC counts units, so a cheaper Huawei inference chip counts the same as an Nvidia H200, and Nvidia’s share by value is likely higher. Infra & Chips.titleZh: DCF Global: The Nordics' AI Boom Meets the Power Test | Data Center Frontier
Infra & Chips.content: Finland's grid operator reports nearly 5 GW of eventual data center capacity associated with signed connection agreements, underscoring the scale of the country's AI infrastructure ambitions. JLL, CBRE, Cushman & Wakefield and datacenterHawk research points to growing Nordic investment appeal, alongside significant questions about power availability, preleasing and project execution. The region's experience offers an increasingly relevant comparison with North America, where power delivery, infrastructure costs and community acceptance are similarly reshaping data center development. The Nordic countries have long occupied a distinctive position in the global data center industry. Their appeal rests on a familiar combination of cool climates, comparatively abundant low-carbon electricity, political stability, and sophisticated energy and communications infrastructure. Now, the accelerating demand for AI computing is transforming that established proposition into something considerably larger. Across Finland, Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Iceland, hyperscalers, AI cloud providers, infrastructure developers and institutional investors are advancing a new generation of high-density data center projects. Their ambitions increasingly extend beyond conventional cloud regions and enterprise colocation into multihundred-megawatt AI campuses and integrated energy infrastructure. The scale of that transformation is particularly evident in Finland, where the country's transmission system operator, Fingrid, reported in August that data center projects with signed grid-connection agreements represented nearly 5 gigawatts of planned eventual capacity. That figure encompasses projects connected to transmission and distribution networks. It does not represent operating data center capacity, nor does a connection agreement guarantee that a project will be completed at its proposed size. Nevertheless, it illustrates the extraordinary volume of investment now being directed toward a country that, until recently, occupied a secondary position behind Sweden and Norway in the Nordic data center market. The acceleration comes with a paradox. The electricity resources, industrial sites and favorable environmental conditions attracting AI developers are also becoming subjects of increasingly consequential public-policy decisions. Finland has raised electricity taxes on data centers and is considering changes to grid-connection priorities. Denmark has already introduced a system that places most large data center projects in a lower-priority category for constrained grid capacity. Meanwhile, investment continues to accelerate. For the Nordics, the central question is no longer whether the region can attract AI infrastructure development. It is how much of the announced capacity can be financed, permitted, connected and ultimately brought into production without compromising the energy-system advantages and sustainability commitments on which the market's appeal depends. The strongest evidence of Finland's changing position came in September, when Google announced plans to invest €13 billion in Finnish digital infrastructure and related projects over 2027 and 2028. The investment encompasses operations and planned development in Hamina, Muhos, Vaala and Kajaani, extending Google's presence beyond its established Hamina campus. Infra & Chips.content: [Cloud](/cloud) # The Five Nine: Why AI’s next bottleneck is memory, not GPUs By [Diana Goovaerts](/person/diana-goovaerts-2) Oct 16, 2026 11:15am [The Five Nine](/keyword/five-nine) [podcast](/keyword/podcast) [Nvidia](/keyword/nvidia) [WEKA](/keyword/weka) AI’s next big bottleneck may not be compute — it may be memory. As enterprises move from training massive models to running inference at scale, the infrastructure challenge is shifting from simply getting enough GPUs to keeping those GPUs fed with data fast enough to make the investment pay off. In this episode of *The Five Nine*, we dig into the memory squeeze with Nvidia’s Jason Hardy and WEKA’s Val Bercovivi, looking at why AI workloads are becoming memory-bound, how agents and KV cache are changing infrastructure economics, and why a GPU cluster optimized for training may not be the right answer for inference. From high-bandwidth memory and storage tiering to GPU Direct Storage and cache-read token pricing, the conversation unpacks what has to change as AI moves into its next phase. The big question: can companies make inference profitable without overbuying the world’s most expensive compute?
